la:noun:sol.html:
sōl, sōlis, m.
Sanscr. svar, shine; cf. Gr. Σείριος, σείρ, σέλας, Ἑλένη; and Lat. serenus
.
Sing., the sun, as a heavenly body.
In gen.: tempora duorum generum sunt, unum annale, quod sol circuitu suo finit,: solis cursus lunaeque meatus,: annum ad cursum solis accommodavit,: liquidi fons luminis aetherius sol,: quid potest esse sole majus?: illud dubium esse nulli potest quin arcus imago solis sit,.—
Esp.
Sol oriens or solis ortus, the east, as a quarter of the heavens: spectant in septemtrionem et orientem solem,; ; ; cf.: a sole exoriente supra Maeotis paludes, Cic. poët. Tusc. 5, 17, 49: si illud signum solis ortum conspiceret,: facem stellae ab ortu solis ad occidentem porrigi visam,: ab ortu solis flare venti,.—
Sol occidens or solis occasus, the west: alterum (litus) vergit ad solem occidentem,: laborant ut spectent sua triclinaria ad solem occidentem,: spectat inter occasum solis et septemtriones,north-west,: quae (pars insulae) est propius solis occasum,.—Cf. poet.: sub sole cadente,.—In phrases, sol is often omitted by ellipsis: unde sol oritur oriens nuncupatur aut ortus; quo demergitur occidens vel occasus,; v. orior, ortus, occĭdo.—
Sol oriens or sol (solis) ortus=sunrise; sol occidens or solis (sol) occasus = sunset: qui solem nec occidentem umquam viderint, nec orientem,: sole orto Gracchus copias educit,: prius orto Sole,: certi solis lunaeque et ortus et occasus sunt,: numquam ab orto sole ad occidentem ... a curiā abscessit,: ut, equis insidentes, solis ortu cursum in quemdam locum dirigerent,ext.: solis occasu,; : ad (sub) solis occasum,towards sunset,; : in occasum declivi sole,.—Poet.: surgente a sole,.—For sol occasus, v. occidere, and (ante solem occasum); (ad solem occasum); cf.: ab exortu ad occasum perstare contuentis solem,.—
To designate a clime, country, etc., as eastern or southern (post-Aug.): ille Liberi currus triumphantem usque ad Thebas a solis ortu vehat,: terminos civitatis nostrae cum sole metimur, (31), 1. it tamen ultra oceanum solemque, : sub alio sole,in another clime,; cf.: ut sua orientis occidentisque terminis finiat (sc. solis),.—
Trop., of a great good or a great man: sol excidisse mihi e mundo videtur,: solem e mundo tollere videntur qui, etc.,: P. Africanus, sol alter (with sole geminato),; cf. : neque mundum posse duobus solibus regi, neque orbem, etc.,.—
Prov.: et sceleratis sol oritur,; cf.: qui solem suum oriri facit super bonos et malos,: nondum omnium dierum sol occidit (Germ. Es ist noch nicht aller Tage Abend) = there are more days yet to come, sc. when the tables may be turned, .—
The poets reckon time in many ways by the movement, etc., of the sun: bis me sol adiit gelidae post frigora brumae,two years,: donec sol annuus omnes conficeret metas,within a year,; cf. : octavo lumine solis,on the eighth day,: sol septimus,: cum sol Herculei terga leonis adit,in midsummer,: O sol Pulcher, O laudande (= dies; sc. Augusti reditus),; cf. : supremo sole,at noon,: sub medium solem,; cf. : sol abit,it is growing late,; cf.: a primo ad ultimum solem,all day long,.—
Transf., the sun, sunlight, sunshine, heat of the sun: ager soli ostentus,exposed to the sun,: sarmenta imponito quae frigus defendant et solem, (49): uvas ponite in sole biduum, (113): sol semper hic est a mani ad vesperum,: quin exta inspicere in sole etiam vivo licet,: nec res posse in sole videri, ni, etc.,: nunc quidem paululum a sole,out of the sun,: cum in sole ambulem,: apricatio in illo Lucretino tuo sole,; cf. : iter in calescente sole factum erat,: torrente meridiano sole,: ex vehementi sole,: urente assiduo sole,: ut veniens dextrum latus aspiciat sol,light of the morning sun,: reformidant insuetum lumina solem,; cf.: nam et solem lumina aegra formidant,: adversi solis ab ictu,sunstroke,: altera (spelunca) solem non recipit,: sole correptis,: pisces, quos sole torreant,: siccatur in sole,: in agmine (Caesar) anteibat capite detecto, seu sol seu imber esset,: patiens pulveris atque solis,.— And trop.: in solem ac pulverem procedere, or producere, into heat and dust, i. e. into practical life (opp. umbra eruditorum), ; .—In a similar sense: cedat stilus gladio, umbra soli,.—Prov.: clarior quam solis radii,: sole ipso est clarius,, n. 47; cf. the class. luce clarius, and: cum id solis luce videatur clarius,.
Plur.
Suns, images of the sun (class.): neque pauci neque leves sunt qui se duo soles vidisse dicant,: Albae duos soles visos ferebant,: et rursus plures soles simul cernuntur,: quid eas vocem? imagines solis? Historici soles vocant, et binos ternosque adparuisse memoriae tradunt,.—
Poet. = days (v. I. C.): nec tamen illis solibus ulla comparebat avis,: saepe ego longos Cantando puerum memini me condere soles,to spend the long summer days in singing,: tres soles ... Erramus,; cf. : Bajani soles,the sunny days of Bajœ,: O soles!: soles fulsere quondam tibi candidi, : soles occidere et redire possunt,: longis solibus,: solibus arctis,short winter days,.—So, to describe certain seasons: solibus hibernis ... gratior,than the sun in winter,: si numeres anno soles et nubila toto,the sunny and cloudy days,.—
Light or heat of the sun (poet. and in postAug. prose; cf. D. supra): pars terrai perusta solibus assiduis,; cf. : pluviis et solibus icta,: quae carent ventis et solibus,i. e. are buried,; : et soles melius nitent,; cf. : ex imbri soles Prospicere ... poteris,: inque novos soles audent se gramina tuto Credere,; similarly,; ; ; : tum blandi soles,: frigore soles juvant,; so : Romulus et frater ... Solibus et campo corpora nuda dabant,: aequora semper solibus orba tument,: solibus rupta glacies,: geminā pereunt caligine soles,: aestivos quo decipis aere soles?: tacent exhausti solibus amnes,; ; ; ; ; : cura soles assiduo quaerendi,: perpeti soles,: evitatis solibus,: (sal) siccatur aestivis solibus,: merguntur in aquam solibus tepefactam,: nec campi minus soles accipiunt,: sarculatio novos soles admittit,; cf. ; : aurea pellebant tepidos umbracula soles,: dum patula defendimus arbore soles,.—Very rarely of the sun's revolution, without reference to light or heat: quae via soles praecipitet,.—In class. prose sometimes solis ardores, with the force of the poet. soles: et nimios solis defendit ardores,; cf.: propter nimios solis ardores,.
Sol, the Sun-god.
Lit.
The ancient Italian deity Sol, represented as driving the four-horse sun-chariot from east to west; later identified with the Greek Helios, and hence often called Titan or Phœbus by the poets: signi dic quid est? Cum quadrigis Sol exoriens,: Sol ... aeternam suscepit lampada mundi,: rapax vis Solis equorum,: quod magni filia Solis eram,; : Solis currus,: secundum (invocabis) Solem et Lunam,: grates tibi ago, summe Sol,: Sol Phaëthonti filio facturum se esse dixit quidquid optasset,: Quid? illum filium Solis nonne patris ipsius luce indignum putas?: qui Solem aurigando aequiperare existimaretur,: Solis colossus Rhodi,; .—Comic.: credo edepol equidem dormire Solem atque adpotum probe,.—
The Phœnician sun-god Heliogabalus (Elagabal), whose worship was introduced by the later emperors (Aurelianus, Heliogabalus): ad templum Heliogabali tetendit ... et Romae Soli templum posuit,; cf. ; 14; 35; 39; ; ; afterwards called Sol Invictus, whose birthday, acc. to the Calendar. Const., was celebrated December 25th; cf. .—
Of the sun-worship of other nations: (Germani) deorum numero ducunt Solem et Vulcanum et Lunam,; cf.: rex regum, frater Solis et Lunae,of the king of Persia,.—
The sun-god as emblem of omniscience: non potuit reperire, si ipsi Soli quaerundas dares, lepidiores ad hanc rem quam ego dabo,: meliorem neque tu reperis, neque Sol videt,: at vigiles mundi ... Sol et Luna,: si hoc uno quicquam Sol vidisset iniquius,: O Solem ipsum beatissimum, qui antequam se abderet fugientem vidit Antonium,: Solem consule, qui late facta diurna videt,: quis Solem fallere possit?; cf. ; .—Hence represented as betrayer of conspiracies: propiusque honos

Boli, qui occulta conjurationis retexisset, ; to him was commended the detection of murderers, in inscriptions over the slain: SOL, TIBI COMMENDO QVI MANVS INTVLIT EI,: SOL, TV INDICES EIVS MORTEM,.—

Poet., to describe the times of the day: solverat flagrantes Sol pronus equos, = it was night, : Sol operum medius summo librabat Olympo Lucentes, ceu staret, equos, = it was mid-day, .
In gen., solis as an appellation.
DIES SOLIS, Sunday (late Lat.), .—
Solis gemma, a precious stone, .—
Solis insula, off the coast of Gedrosia, ; .—
Solis fons, in Marmorica, ; Mela, 1, 8, 1; .—
Solis promunturium, in Africa, .—
Solis oppidum, a town in Ægina, .
